One country, 330.8 million people, three ways to draw it

The 50 states by 2020 Census P1 resident population — California 39,538,223 down to Wyoming 576,851, a 68.5× range — rendered three ways in Vega-Lite: the true map, a Demers square cartogram, and an equal-tile mosaic. Same data, same colour scale; only the geometry changes.

Hover any state — it lights up in all three views, with its population and land area in the infotip.
Hover a state in any view to pin its numbers here.

1 · Reference map

Area = land. Colour = population.

Undistorted Albers USA from the 2024 Cartographic Boundary Files (1:5,000,000). This is the map the other two are judged against — and the one where Wyoming outweighs New Jersey.

Geography is honest here; the data isn’t. Land area and population share almost nothing — Texas is 35.5× New Jersey’s land with only 3.1× its people.

2 · Demers squares

Square area = population. Colour = population.

One square per state, side proportional to √population, laid out from each state’s Albers centroid with overlaps removed. California is a square 148 units wide; Wyoming, 18.

0 overlaps. Mean displacement from the true centroid 83.5 km (max 482.5 km, New York); east–west ordering preserved for 98.8% of state pairs, north–south 95.7%.

3 · Mosaic tile grid

One equal tile per state. Colour = population.

Every state gets the same square on a 12×9 grid (the amCharts tile-map layout). Area says nothing here — the 68.5× skew lives entirely in the colour.

Preserves 53 of 107 true geographic adjacencies (49.5%), with 19 false adjacencies — grid neighbours that don’t actually touch.

Area-to-value legend — read the Demers squares against this

Squares drawn at exactly the Demers view’s scale. Area judgement is unreliable by eye — perception compresses area differences — so anchor on these before comparing squares.

What each view costs you

No cartogram gets zero statistical error, perfect shapes, and intact adjacencies at once — Alam, Kobourov & Veeramoni’s impossibility result. These are the trade-offs in this test, stated plainly.

Demers here is a baseline, not the LP

The squares were placed by iterative overlap removal — an FRC-style force baseline — not by Nickel et al.’s TOP-W-St linear program. Side² is exactly proportional to population and the verified layout has zero overlaps, but the H/V separation constraints are not enforced as hard constraints.

That means Lemma 1 does not apply: there is no guarantee that interpolating between this layout and another metric’s layout stays overlap-free, so smooth animated metric-switching would need the LP solved properly first.

The tile grid spends area to buy equality

One tile per state is the right call when each unit counts the same — a seat, a vote, a district. But it discards the area encoding entirely and keeps only about half the true adjacencies (53/107), while inventing 19 that don’t exist. Shape survives only as the familiar silhouette of the grid.

No contiguous cartogram in this test — deliberately

A 2020 contiguous diffusion cartogram can’t be computed in a Vega-Lite spec. Classical diffusion takes 25–50 s on a 1024×1024 grid (Alam et al.), and the fast flow-based route, go-cart.io, is interactive-only — a browser workflow with server-side compute, no precomputed 2020 export to embed.

The one fetchable precomputed file was checked and rejected: it encodes 2014 estimates, not 2020 Census values, and fails the area check (mean absolute relative area error 50%; Montana +406%). It is kept in the dataset folder as evidence, not rendered here as if it were the real thing.

Data. Populations: 2020 Census, 119th Congressional District Summary File, Table P1 (resident population), cross-checked against the 2020 Apportionment Table A with zero mismatches. Boundaries: U.S. Census Bureau 2024 Cartographic Boundary Files, 1:5,000,000. Demers layout: side = 0.023606·√population in a 960×600 view fitted from EPSG:5070 centroids, minimum gap 2 units, AK/HI as Albers-USA-style insets. Tile grid: amCharts US tile-map layout, DC dropped.

Literature. Alam, Kobourov & Veeramoni (2015), Quantitative Measures for Cartogram Generation Techniques; Duncan & Gastner (2024), go-cart.io, PLOS ONE 19(5); Nickel et al. (2022), Multicriteria Optimization for Dynamic Demers Cartograms; Nusrat & Kobourov (2016), The State of the Art in Cartograms. Juxtaposed reference map, linked highlighting, infotips, and the square area-to-value legend follow the interaction patterns those papers recommend.
